Matière noire ne veut pas dire trous noi: Dark matter doesn't mean black holes or dark clouds: those would be ordinary matter.
Rocheuses près du Soleil (Mercure, Vénus: Rocky planets close to the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars), giants beyond (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), asteroids between the two groups.
Entre Mars et Jupiter s'étend la ceintur: Between Mars and Jupiter lies the main asteroid belt, millions of rocks whose total mass is only a few percent of the Moon's. Jupiter, the largest planet, alone outweighs all the others combined more than twice over.
Pourquoi Pluton n'est plus une planète: Why Pluto is no longer a planet

Pluto ticks the first two boxes but not the third: it shares its zone with a crowd of icy objects in the Kuiper belt.
Elle est donc devenue une planète naine,: So it became a dwarf planet, like Ceres in the asteroid belt. Pluto did not change; the definition arrived.
La distance au Soleil ne fait pas tout :: Distance from the Sun is not everything: the atmosphere matters. Venus (≈ 465 °C) beats Mercury thanks to its greenhouse effect.
Mars, elle, est rouge parce que sa pouss: Mars, for its part, is red because its dust contains iron oxide: rust, in short.
Saisons = inclinaison de l'axe (23,4°),: Seasons = axial tilt (23.4°), not distance. New moon = the Moon between Earth and the Sun.
La Lune nous montre toujours la même fac: The Moon always shows us the same face, because it spins on itself in exactly the time it takes to go around Earth. When it passes between us and the Sun, its lit side faces away from us: that is the new moon.
Étoile = fusion de l'hydrogène en hélium: Star = hydrogen fusing into helium in the core. Blue = very hot, red = cooler.
Sa couleur trahit sa température de surf: Its colour gives away its surface temperature, the opposite of taps: blue stars exceed 10,000 °C, red ones are around 3,000 °C, and the Sun, at about 5,500 °C, is yellow-white.
Soleil : géante rouge puis naine blanche: Sun: red giant then white dwarf. Massive stars: supernova. Gold comes from stellar explosions and collisions.
Quand l'hydrogène du cœur s'épuise, l'ét: When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the star swells. The Sun, in about 5 billion years, will become a red giant, then shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf: a core about as massive as the Sun but the size of Earth. A spoonful of its matter would weigh tonnes.
Les étoiles bien plus massives finissent: Much more massive stars end as supernovae, an explosion that leaves a neutron star or a black hole. These explosions, and above all collisions of neutron stars such as the one observed in 2017 (GW170817), make gold and the other very heavy elements.
Regarder loin, c'est regarder le passé: Looking far is looking into the past
1 light-year ≈ 9,460 billion km. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star, is 4.2 ly away.
Les étoiles scintillent parce que la tur: Stars twinkle because air turbulence keeps bending their light; seen from space, they do not twinkle.
La Polaire montre le nord, Sirius est la: Polaris shows north, Sirius is the brightest. 88 constellations, figures in perspective.
L'étoile Polaire est presque dans l'axe: Polaris lies almost on Earth's axis of rotation, above the North Pole: it shows north and seems still while the sky turns. But it is not the brightest; that is Sirius.
Ellipses, Soleil au foyer ; plus vite pr: Ellipses with the Sun at a focus; faster near the Sun; T² ∝ a³.
En 1609, à partir des mesures de Tycho B: In 1609, from Tycho Brahe's measurements of Mars, Johannes Kepler showed that planets do not move in circles: they trace ellipses with the Sun at one focus. Second law: the Sun-planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet moves faster near the Sun.
La troisième loi, en 1619, relie la duré: The third law, in 1619, links the orbital period to the size of the orbit: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, T² ∝ a³. The farther out, the longer the lap.
Une orbite, c'est une chute qui rate le: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground
Orbite basse ≈ 7,8 km/s ; libération 11,: Low orbit ≈ 7.8 km/s; escape 11.2 km/s. In the ISS gravity is ≈ 90 %: people float because they are falling.
Là-haut, la gravité vaut encore environ: Up there, gravity is still about 90 % of what it is on the ground. Astronauts float because they fall together with their station, not because gravity is gone. To escape Earth without an engine takes 11.2 km/s, the escape velocity.
Marées surtout dues à la Lune. Géostatio: Tides mostly due to the Moon. Geostationary: ≈ 35,800 km, one lap per day.
Plus un satellite est proche, plus il to: The closer a satellite, the faster it goes round: 1 h 30 min for the Station, 27 days for the Moon. At about 35,800 km, a satellite takes exactly one day per lap: it stays above the same point on the equator; it is geostationary.
Neptune a été trouvée par le calcul (Le: Neptune was found by calculation (Le Verrier, 1846). Black hole: not even light escapes; first image in 2019.
La gravité permet de prédire ce qu'on n': Gravity lets us predict what has not yet been seen. In 1846, Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unknown planet disturbing Uranus must be; Johann Galle found it on the night of 23-24 September, less than one degree from the predicted spot: Neptune.
Un trou noir est une région où la gravit: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. Seen from afar, it attracts like any equal mass; it does not suck in anything extra. The first image of a black hole, M87*, dates from 2019.
Voie lactée : spirale de 100 à 400 milli: Milky Way: a spiral of 100 to 400 billion stars, black hole Sagittarius A* at the centre. Andromeda is another galaxy (Hubble).
Le Soleil est une étoile parmi 100 à 400: The Sun is one star among 100 to 400 billion in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy: a flattened disc with arms. We are in one arm, about 26,000 to 27,000 light-years from the centre, where a supermassive black hole hides, Sagittarius A*, about 4 million solar masses.
En 1923-1924, Edwin Hubble repère une ét: In 1923-1924, Edwin Hubble spotted a variable star in Andromeda, measured its distance and proved it was another galaxy. Andromeda is approaching us at about 110 km/s: the two galaxies should merge in a few billion years.
Décalage vers le rouge = éloignement. Pl: Redshift = moving away. Farther means faster (Hubble-Lemaître). Space stretches with no centre.
La lumière des galaxies lointaines est d: The light of distant galaxies is shifted towards red: they are moving away, and the farther they are, the faster. Georges Lemaître proposed it in 1927, Hubble measured it in 1929: this is the Hubble-Lemaître law.
Attention à l'image : les galaxies ne fu: Beware the image: galaxies are not fleeing through space from a centre. Space itself is stretching, everywhere at once, like raisin bread rising.
Le Big Bang n'est pas une explosion: The Big Bang is not an explosion
Âge : 13,8 milliards d'années. Fond diff: Age: 13.8 billion years. Background radiation: light emitted 380,000 years later, discovered in 1965.
Il y a environ 13,8 milliards d'années,: About 13.8 billion years ago, the Universe was extremely hot and dense, and it has been expanding ever since. Lemaître spoke in 1931 of a 'primeval atom'; the name 'Big Bang' comes from Fred Hoyle, who mocked it on the radio in 1949.
La preuve la plus forte : le fond diffus: The strongest evidence: the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the Universe, emitted about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Penzias and Wilson picked it up by chance in 1965, first suspected pigeon droppings in their antenna, and received the Nobel Prize in 1978.
Le ciel tourne parce que la Terre tourne: The sky turns because Earth turns (Foucault pendulum, 1851). Lunar cycle ≈ 29.5 days. Shooting star = burning dust.
Les étoiles semblent tourner autour de n: Stars seem to turn around us at night because Earth is spinning. Léon Foucault showed it in 1851 with his pendulum, whose plane of swing slowly rotates over the hours. The whole sky appears to pivot around Polaris, almost fixed above the North Pole.
Les phases de la Lune reviennent tous le: The Moon's phases repeat every 29.5 days or so, the synodic month. And a shooting star is not a star: it is a grain of dust burning up as it enters the atmosphere. The August Perseids are debris from comet Swift-Tuttle.
1 ua ≈ 150 millions de km ; 1 année-lumi: 1 AU ≈ 150 million km; 1 light-year ≈ 9,460 billion km. 88 constellations, boundaries set in 1930.
Deux unités à ne pas confondre. L'unité: Two units not to mix up. The astronomical unit, about 150 million km, is the average Earth-Sun distance: handy within the Solar System. The light-year, about 9,460 billion km, is the distance light travels in a year: handy between stars.
Les 88 constellations reconnues par l'Un: The 88 constellations recognised by the International Astronomical Union were given official boundaries in 1930: every point in the sky belongs to exactly one constellation.
Grand miroir = objets plus faibles. Newt: Bigger mirror = fainter objects. Newton, 1668: first mirror telescope. James Webb (2021): infrared.
Un télescope sert d'abord à collecter de: A telescope is first of all a light collector: the bigger the mirror, the fainter the objects it can see. Isaac Newton built the first mirror telescope in 1668, to avoid the coloured fringes that lenses produce.
Le télescope spatial James Webb, lancé e: The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, observes mainly in the infrared. Light from very distant galaxies is so redshifted that it arrives as infrared: that is where to look to see the first galaxies.
Spoutnik 1957, Gagarine 1961 (108 min),: Sputnik 1957, Gagarin 1961 (108 min), Tereshkova 1963, Apollo 11 in 1969; 12 people on the Moon.
Le 4 octobre 1957, l'URSS lance Spoutnik: On 4 October 1957, the USSR launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, which sent out a simple radio beep. On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space: a single orbit in 108 minutes. In June 1963, Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, aboard Vostok 6.
Les États-Unis répondent avec Apollo : A: The United States answered with Apollo: Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon in July 1969. From 1969 to 1972, six Apollo missions put twelve people on it in all.
Fusée = action-réaction, pas d'appui sur: Rocket = action-reaction, no pushing on air. Tsiolkovsky's equation (1903). Low orbit ≈ 7.8 km/s.
Une fusée n'a pas besoin d'air pour pous: A rocket does not need air to push against: it throws gas out backwards very fast, and that gas pushes it forwards. That is Newton's third law, action and reaction. It even works better in a vacuum.
En 1903, le professeur russe Konstantin: In 1903, Russian teacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky set out the rocket equation, which links the speed gained to the exhaust speed and the share of fuel. To stay in low orbit you need about 7.8 km/s, nearly 28,000 km/h.
Katherine Johnson a vérifié le vol de Gl: Katherine Johnson checked Glenn's flight (1962). Voyager 1: the farthest, outside the heliosphere since 2012. Perseverance: Jezero crater.
Lancée en 1977, la sonde Voyager 1 a qui: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 left the Sun's bubble, the heliosphere, in 2012: it is the most distant human-made object, with a golden record on board. On Mars, the Perseverance rover has been exploring Jezero crater since 2021, sampling rocks that might hold traces of ancient life.
51 Pegasi b (Mayor et Queloz, 1995, Nobe: 51 Pegasi b (Mayor and Queloz, 1995, Nobel 2019). Over 5,000 confirmed by 2022. TRAPPIST-1: 7 Earth-sized planets.
Une exoplanète est une planète qui tourn: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found the first one around a Sun-like star: 51 Pegasi b, a scorching gas giant hugging its star. They received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
Depuis, la chasse s'est emballée : le ca: Since then the hunt has taken off: the 5,000 confirmed exoplanets mark was passed in 2022, according to NASA. The TRAPPIST-1 system, announced in 2017, alone has seven Earth-sized planets, and the star closest to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, has its own planet, Proxima b.
Transit = petite baisse de lumière quand: Transit = slight dip in light as the planet passes in front. Radial velocity = the star's wobble, measured with the Doppler effect.
On ne voit presque jamais une exoplanète: We almost never see an exoplanet directly: its star outshines it. We spot it by its effects. Transit method: when the planet passes in front of its star, the light dims very slightly, at regular intervals. The Kepler space telescope found thousands this way.
Zone habitable = eau liquide possible, p: Habitable zone = liquid water possible, life not guaranteed. Biosignature = chemical hint of life. Europa and Enceladus: oceans under ice.
La zone habitable d'une étoile est la ba: A star's habitable zone is the band of distances where water could stay liquid on a planet's surface: neither too close nor too far. It is a favourable condition, not a guarantee: a planet can sit there and still be a desert.
Équation de Drake (1961) : estimer les c: Drake equation (1961): estimating civilisations. Fermi paradox (1950): so where are they? The Wow! signal (1977) was never heard again.
En 1961, Frank Drake écrit une équation: In 1961, Frank Drake wrote an equation to estimate the number of civilisations able to communicate in our Galaxy: the number of stars, the share with planets, the share where life appears, and so on. Its terms are so uncertain that estimates range from one to millions.
Lors d'un déjeuner à Los Alamos en 1950,: At a lunch in Los Alamos in 1950, Enrico Fermi reportedly asked: 'But where is everybody?' If so many civilisations are possible, why no sign of them? That is the Fermi paradox. The only famous candidate, the 'Wow!' signal picked up in 1977, was never heard again.
Zwicky (1933, amas de Coma) puis Vera Ru: Zwicky (1933, Coma cluster) then Vera Rubin (1970s, galaxy edges too fast): mass is missing.
En 1933, Fritz Zwicky observe que les ga: In 1933, Fritz Zwicky noticed that galaxies in the Coma cluster were moving too fast: the visible mass was not enough to hold them together. He spoke of dunkle Materie, dark matter.
Dans les années 1970, Vera Rubin mesure: In the 1970s, Vera Rubin measured how galaxies rotate: stars at the edge spin as fast as those near the centre, when they should slow down, like distant planets around the Sun. An invisible mass is needed, in a halo around each galaxy.
Voir l'invisible par sa gravité: Seeing the invisible through its gravity
Matière noire = invisible, détectée par: Dark matter = invisible, detected through its gravity (lensing). Bullet Cluster (2006): mass and gas separated.
La matière noire n'émet ni n'absorbe de: Dark matter neither emits nor absorbs light: it is detected only through its gravity. Its mass bends the light of galaxies behind it, like a magnifying glass: these are gravitational lenses, a prediction of general relativity that lets us map it.
L'amas de la Balle, observé en 2006, est: The Bullet Cluster, observed in 2006, is a strong argument: two clusters collided, their gas was slowed in the middle, but most of the mass, measured by lensing, carried straight on. So the mass is not where the visible matter is.
L'énergie noire et le grand inventaire: Dark energy and the grand inventory
Énergie noire : expansion qui accélère (: Dark energy: accelerating expansion (1998). Inventory: 5 % ordinary matter, 27 % dark matter, 68 % dark energy.
En 1998, deux équipes mesurent des super: In 1998, two teams measured distant supernovae and found that the Universe's expansion is speeding up instead of slowing down. Whatever drives it is called dark energy; Nobel Prize in 2011. Einstein had introduced a cosmological constant to get a static Universe, then dropped it: it is back to describe this energy.
Selon le satellite Planck, l'Univers, âg: According to the Planck satellite, the Universe, 13.8 billion years old, contains about 5 % ordinary matter, 27 % dark matter and 68 % dark energy. And dark matter is not made of ordinary black holes: its nature remains unknown, and candidate particles such as WIMPs have never been detected.
Mercure est la plus proche du Soleil, el: Mercury is closest to the Sun and goes around it in 88 days. Yet the hottest planet is Venus: about 465 °C at the surface, night included. Its very thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps the heat, a greenhouse effect pushed to the extreme. We have known it first-hand since 15 December 1970: the Soviet probe Venera 7 landed on Venus and sent back, for the first time, data from the surface of another planet.
La Terre tourne autour du Soleil en envi: Earth goes around the Sun in about 365.25 days: the extra quarter day explains the leap year. Seasons do not come from the distance to the Sun, since Earth is closest to it in early January, in the middle of the northern winter. They come from the tilt of its axis, about 23.4°: in summer, our hemisphere gets the Sun higher in the sky and for longer. As for leap years, because the year is a little shorter than 365.25 days, Pope Gregory XIII reformed the calendar with a bull of 24 February 1582: century years are leap years only if divisible by 400. 2000 was, 1900 was not.
Une étoile est une boule de gaz si massi: A star is a ball of gas so massive that its core is crushed and heated to millions of degrees. There, about 15 million degrees for the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and release energy: that is nuclear fusion. Why stars shine remained a puzzle until 1938, when Hans Bethe described the fusion reactions that power them, work that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1967.
L'année-lumière est une distance, pas un: A light-year is a distance, not a duration: how far light travels in a year, about 9,460 billion km. The star closest to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away: we see it as it was more than four years ago. That light takes time to travel was shown by the Dane Ole Rømer in 1676: the eclipses of Io, a moon of Jupiter, come late when Earth moves away from Jupiter. He estimated it took about 22 minutes to cross Earth's orbit; it is closer to 17.
Newton l'a compris : la Lune tombe sans: Newton understood it: the Moon keeps falling towards Earth, but it moves sideways so fast that it always misses. Staying in low orbit takes about 7.8 km/s; the Space Station, 400 km up, thus circles Earth in about 92 minutes. The first human-made object to fall around the Earth this way was Sputnik 1, launched by the USSR on 4 October 1957: it went round in about 96 minutes.
La Lune tire plus fort sur le côté de la: The Moon pulls harder on the side of Earth facing it than on the far side: the oceans stretch, and those are the tides. The Sun plays a part too, less strongly; when Sun and Moon line up, we get the large spring tides. Newton gave the explanation in 1687 in his Principia: tides come from the pull of the Moon and the Sun on the Earth's waters.
Méthode des vitesses radiales : la planè: Radial velocity method: the planet and its star orbit their shared centre of mass, so the star wobbles slightly back and forth. This is measured through the Doppler effect: its light turns bluer as it approaches and redder as it recedes. That is how 51 Pegasi b was found. Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced it on 6 October 1995, using the ELODIE spectrograph at the Haute-Provence Observatory: the first planet found around a Sun-like star. Nobel Prize in Physics 2019.
Pour trahir la vie de loin, on cherche d: To detect life from afar, we look for biosignatures, such as certain gases in an atmosphere: oxygen and methane together, for example, destroy each other and are hard to sustain without life. The idea comes from James Lovelock, in 1965 in the journal Nature, while he was thinking for NASA about detecting life on Mars: an atmosphere far from chemical equilibrium betrays life. Closer to home, Europa, a moon of Jupiter, hides a salty ocean beneath its ice, as does Enceladus around Saturn: serious candidates for microbial life.
Une constellation est une figure en pers: A constellation is a figure in perspective: stars that look close together from here but can be at very different distances. The International Astronomical Union recognises 88. It fixed the list in 1922, and their boundaries, drawn by the Belgian Eugène Delporte, were adopted in 1928 and published in 1930: every point of the sky belongs to exactly one constellation.
Eight planets orbit the Sun. The four closest, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. The next four are giants: Jupiter and Saturn, made mostly of hydrogen and helium, then Uranus and Neptune, rich in ices. For millennia only six were known, Earth included. The oldest written trace of a planet being tracked is the Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa: the risings and settings of Venus recorded over 21 years, compiled in Babylon around the mid-17th century BCE. The copy that survives, a clay tablet from the 7th century BCE found in the library of Nineveh, is in the British Museum. On 13 March 1781, William Herschel spotted Uranus from his garden in Bath with a telescope he had built; he first took it for a comet. It was the first planet discovered since antiquity.
